facts.raw_span: A 60-year-old Saudi man presented with an 18-month history of erythroderma affecting his entire body and face
slightly pruritic, slowly progressive erythematous lesions on his trunk and retroauricular area
confluent lichenified erythromelanotic plaques with overlying thick greasy scales on the face, neck, trunk, genitalia, upper and lower extremities, palms, and soles
sparing of the nails and scalp
Bilateral lower‐lid ectropion was present
no palpable lymphadenopathy
epidermotropism of a large number of atypical lymphocytes—single and in clusters—and a superficial dermal band‐like lymphocytic infiltrate with dermal fibrosis
Direct immunofluorescence was negative for fibrinogen, C3, IgA, IgM, and IgG
Immunohistochemical staining showed tumor cells positive for CD3 and CD45RO but negative for CD4, CD8, and CD7
CD30 was positive in fewer than 25% of lymphocytes

slightly pruritic, slowly progressive erythematous lesions on his trunk and retroauricular area
confluent lichenified erythromelanotic plaques with overlying thick greasy scales on the face, neck, trunk, genitalia, upper and lower extremities, palms, and soles
sparing of the nails and scalp
Bilateral lower‐lid ectropion was present
no palpable lymphadenopathy
epidermotropism of a large number of atypical lymphocytes—single and in clusters—and a superficial dermal band‐like lymphocytic infiltrate with dermal fibrosis
Direct immunofluorescence was negative for fibrinogen, C3, IgA, IgM, and IgG
Immunohistochemical staining showed tumor cells positive for CD3 and CD45RO but negative for CD4, CD8, and CD7
CD30 was positive in fewer than 25% of lymphocytes

concepts.why: The patient's presentation of erythroderma, confluent lichenified erythromelanotic plaques, and epidermotropism of atypical lymphocytes is consistent with Sézary syndrome, a type of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.

The patient's history of slowly progressive erythematous lesions and the presence of epidermotropism of atypical lymphocytes are consistent with mycosis fungoides, a type of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.
The patient's presentation of erythroderma and epidermotropism of atypical lymphocytes is consistent with cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, but the specific subtype is unclear.

The patient's history of erythematous lesions and the presence of thick greasy scales are consistent with psoriasis, although the absence of other characteristic features and the presence of atypical lymphocytes make this diagnosis less likely.
It explains the presence of bilateral lower-lid ectropion and the specific immunohistochemical staining pattern, including CD30 positivity in fewer than 25% of lymphocytes.
